question: Is sending people into space worth the cost, when robots can do most of the science for far less?
answer: Astronauts fixed Hubble's flawed mirror in 1993 and serviced it four more times, turning a failure into one of the most productive telescopes ever built. People improvise when things break. Crewed missions also win public support and draw young engineers in a way robotic ones rarely do. Science is not the only return worth buying.
move: Whichever side you took, the hinge is whether inspiration counts as a return.
ask: Which of my spending do I justify by how it makes me feel, and is that a fair return?
counterpoint: The International Space Station has cost well over $100 billion, more than ten James Webb telescopes. For that money robots could have visited every planet several times over. Keeping people alive takes most of a crewed mission's mass and budget, and its science per dollar has rarely matched a robotic mission's.
reference: Launius & McCurdy, Robots in Space: Technology, Evolution, and Interplanetary Travel, Johns Hopkins University Press, 2008
